screens.title: Reorder Buffer and In-Order Commit
screens.narratorSegment: Out-of-order execution improves performance by letting independent instructions run ahead, but it complicates how we handle exceptions and branch mispredictions. In this lesson you will learn why imprecise exceptions happen when instructions complete out of program order, and how a Reorder Buffer, or ROB, holds results until they may be safely committed in program order. We will study the fields inside a ROB entry — type, destination, value, ready and speculation bits — and follow the three main phases: dispatch, execute, and commit. You will also see why modern designs use a physical register file with a map table instead of relying only on the ROB for recent values. Finally, we will work through a hands-on simulation of a mispredicted branch so you can see how speculative entries are flushed and how a recovery penalty accumulates. By the end you should be able to explain the ROB's role in precise exceptions and how it supports speculative execution while keeping the architectural state consistent. Consider how ROB size impacts both parallelism and the cost of a misprediction — that trade-off motivates many design choices in real processors.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Reorder Buffer Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Orientation

Reorder Buffer and In-Order Commit

Learn why the ROB is essential to make out-of-order execution safe, how it records results and speculation state, and how commit ensures precise exceptions.

Problem
Imprecise exceptions break recovery because later instructions may have modified the architectural state.
Solution
ROB buffers results until commit, guaranteeing the register file reflects program order and enabling precise exception handling.
What you'll explore
  • ROB fields and ready/speculative bits
  • Dispatch, execute, commit, flush lifecycle
  • Register file vs. physical register file trade-offs
Visual Concept
ROB as a conveyor belt of in-order slots
Head
I1 ready
I2 spec
I3 exec
I4 free
The belt holds instructions in program order. Results are stored in ROB entries until commit; only the head can write architectural state. Flushed entries never touch the register file.
Why precise exceptions
Committing in program order ensures that when an exception is raised, the processor can roll back to a known clean state and transfer control to the OS safely.
Try this
Later we'll simulate a mispredicted branch and count the cycles wasted when speculative entries are flushed.
Explore Key Topics
Dispatch & Reserve
ROB entries allocated in program order and reservation stations hold instructions for execution.
Commit & Exception
Results are written to registers only at commit, enabling precise exception handling and recoverable state.
Speculation & Flush
Speculative entries carry a bit; on mispredict they are discarded and the map table or register file is restored as needed.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson set you will gain four concrete skills. First, you will explain why out-of-order execution complicates exception handling: specifically, how later instructions can alter the architectural state before an earlier fault is detected, producing imprecise exceptions. Second, you will implement a reorder buffer that preserves program order for commits while letting instructions execute out of order; this includes allocating ROB entries at dispatch and writing results into the ROB rather than the register file. Third, you will understand the interaction between the ROB, reservation stations, and the register file or a physical register file with a map table; you'll see how the ROB can be the only place holding a result until commit or how a PRF lets reads bypass the ROB. Fourth, you will describe speculative execution behavior and how the ROB handles mispredictions by marking speculative entries and flushing them on branch resolution. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify your understanding by tracing a misprediction and explaining the recovery steps.

screens.title: Why Out-of-Order Execution Causes Imprecise Exceptions
screens.narratorSegment: An imprecise exception occurs when the processor can no longer guarantee which instruction caused a fault because later instructions have already modified the architectural state. In a sequential design, an exception arises when the offending instruction completes and the processor stops in program order. In contrast, an out-of-order engine may execute and even write results for younger instructions before an older instruction raises an exception. A concrete example: imagine instruction five causes a divide-by-zero, but instruction eight has already written its result to a register. If the processor cannot undo instruction eight's write, the register file no longer reflects the state at the point of instruction five, and the operating system cannot reconstruct a correct program state. That is why imprecise exceptions are unacceptable for general-purpose systems. A common misconception is that simply stopping execution later will be sufficient; it is not, because writes already made by younger instructions persist unless the architecture prevents or delays them. The ROB solves this by buffering writes until commit. Think about this question: if you could snapshot every register at every instruction, would you still need a ROB? The practical cost of full snapshots explains why the ROB is the preferred lightweight solution.

keyIdea.text: Out-of-order completion can hide the faulting instruction; delaying commits preserves a precise architectural state.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Imprecise Exceptions
Definition and example

Imprecise Exception Explained

An imprecise exception means the processor cannot present a program-order-consistent state at the time of a fault. This happens when younger instructions have already updated registers or memory before an older instruction signals an exception.

Concrete example
If I5 faults but I8 already wrote R2, the OS cannot reconstruct registers as they were when I5 was reached. That makes debugging and recovery impossible.
Common misconception
Stopping later is not enough; writes must be prevented from becoming architecturally visible until it is safe to commit.
Key takeaway

Precise exception handling requires that architectural state only changes at in-order commit points. The ROB enforces this rule.

Analogy
Think of program order as a train schedule. If later cars unload passengers before earlier cars arrive, the manifest no longer matches the train's intended order. The ROB keeps the doors closed until the right car reaches the platform.
Check your understanding
  • Why is an imprecise exception harmful to an operating system?
  • What minimal guarantee must a hardware structure provide to avoid imprecise exceptions?

screens.title: What Is a Reorder Buffer (ROB)?
screens.narratorSegment: A Reorder Buffer is a circular, program-ordered buffer that holds instructions from dispatch until commit. Each entry records the instruction type, destination architectural register, computed value, a ready bit indicating execution completion, an exception flag, and a speculation bit. The ROB's central role is to allow instruction execution to proceed out of order while deferring writes to the architectural state until it is safe to apply them in program order. This guarantees precise exceptions and enables simple recovery: if an exception or a misprediction is detected at the head, the processor can flush all later entries without having to undo committed state. A common misconception is that the ROB stores only values; in practice it stores control status too, like exception flags and speculation markers, which are essential for deciding whether to commit an entry. The ROB is a circular structure with head and tail pointers; the tail allocates new entries at dispatch and the head advances on commit. Consider a high-level analogy: the ROB is like a waiting room that records results out of order but only lets people through the exit in order.

keyIdea.title: ROB role
keyIdea.text: A circular buffer that holds results and control metadata until in-order commit ensures precise state updates.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › What is the ROB?

ROB structure and purpose

The ROB records instruction metadata and results until the instruction reaches the head and commits. It prevents younger instructions from making architectural state visible prematurely.

Fields
  • Instruction type
  • Destination register
  • Value and ready bit
  • Exception & speculation bits
Pointers
Head points to the next commit candidate. Tail allocates new entries at dispatch. The circular design reuses slots after commit.
Roles
Buffers results, records speculation, and sequences commits to ensure precise exceptions and recoverability.
Takeaway

The ROB is the single structure responsible for delaying architectural updates until it is safe to apply them in program order.

Quick diagram
[Head] • I1(ready) • I2(spec) • I3(ready) • I4 • [Tail]
Entries contain both data and control flags so commit can decide whether to write results or to flush on mispredict.
Analogy
Think of the ROB as a waiting room where tasks finish work out of order but only pass through the exit in the correct sequence.

screens.title: ROB Operation: Dispatch and Execute
screens.narratorSegment: Dispatch and execution are the first two stages of ROB operation. At dispatch, the processor allocates a ROB entry in program order and places the instruction in a reservation station. The destination register is marked as being produced by that ROB entry, so reads of that architectural register will either read a committed value or the pending ROB result. Execution can proceed out of order inside reservation stations; when an instruction completes there, it writes the computed value into its ROB entry and sets the ready bit. Importantly, the result is not written into the architectural register file at this moment. A concrete example: an ADD dispatched as entry 5 executes earlier than entry 3 in the reservation station and writes its sum into ROB[5]. Later, commit logic will allow ROB[3] and then ROB[5] to write to registers. A common misconception is that reserving the destination in the register file makes writes atomic; instead the ROB keeps the architectural file unchanged until commit. The dispatch/execute split enables high instruction-level parallelism while preserving an ordered commit path for correctness. ROB Operation: Dispatch and Execute means dispatch allocates an ordered rob slot; execute writes results to the rob and sets ready bits without touching architectural state.. In practical terms, how instructions enter the rob and write results back. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Dispatch & execute
keyIdea.text: Dispatch allocates an ordered ROB slot; execute writes results to the ROB and sets ready bits without touching architectural state.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Dispatch & Execute
Steps at a glance
  1. Dispatch: allocate ROB entry at tail and mark destination as pending.
  2. Place in RS: instruction sits in a reservation station until operands are ready.
  3. Execute: instruction executes out of order when operands available.
  4. Write result: write value into ROB entry and set ready bit.
Misconception
Writing a result to the ROB is not the same as writing to the register file; only commit writes to the architectural state.
Visual: Dispatch → Reservation → ROB writeback
Dispatch
Allocate ROB[tail] and update destination mapping so reads can find the pending value.
Reservation Station
Instruction waits for operands. When ready it fires and executes even if older ROB entries are not ready.
ROB Writeback
Result written to ROB entry and ready bit set. Commit will later move the value to the register file in order.
Pro tip
Ensure your simulator writes the value to ROB entries on execution completion so commit logic reads the ready bit, not reservation stations, for commit decisions.

screens.title: Commit and Flush: Making Exceptions Precise
screens.narratorSegment: Commit is the stage where the ROB enforces program order on architectural updates. The commit logic repeatedly checks the head entry: if the head's ready bit is set and no exception is recorded, the ROB writes the entry's value into the register file or commits a store to memory, then advances the head pointer to the next entry. If the head entry has an exception, the processor handles the exception using the precise state at the previous commit point and flushes all subsequent ROB entries. For branch mispredictions, when the branch resolves at or before commit and is found incorrect, all speculative entries after that branch are discarded. A flush discards results stored only in the ROB and restores the register map or register file to match the last committed state. A common error in implementations is to forget to free resources or update the map table only after commit; doing those steps incorrectly breaks recoverability. Think of commit as a gatekeeper: only when the gate opens does the ROB's data become part of the architectural state. What decision does commit make if the head is not ready? It stalls and preserves precise ordering until the instruction completes.

keyIdea.title: Commit & flush
keyIdea.text: Commit writes ROB results to the architecture only at the head; flush discards speculative entries to restore the last committed state.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Commit & Flush

Commit loop and flush mechanics

The commit logic inspects the head entry each cycle. If ready and exception-free, the entry's value becomes architecturally visible and head advances. If the head has an exception or a branch misprediction is detected at commit, all later entries are flushed and the processor restores the last committed state.

When to stall
If the head is not ready, commit stalls until it becomes ready. This enforces in-order visibility regardless of execution completion order.
Flush behavior
On mispredict or exception, discard all entries after the faulting entry so none of their results reach the register file or memory.
Common mistake
Not restoring the register map or freeing physical registers correctly during a flush will leave the architectural state inconsistent and break precise recovery.
Mini checklist
  • Check head.ready
  • If ready, write to register or memory
  • If exception, handle and flush subsequent entries
Key takeaway
Commit makes the final correctness decision; flush preserves recoverability by discarding uncommitted work.

screens.title: ROB with Register File vs. ROB with Physical Register File (PRF)
screens.narratorSegment: There are two common approaches to holding in-flight results: keeping the ROB as the only source of pending results, or using a physical register file with a register map table. In the ROB-with-register-file approach, the ROB stores results until commit, and the register file always reflects only committed values. Reading a register requires checking the ROB to find the most recent uncommitted write. This searching can be slow and power hungry. The alternative, a Physical Register File (PRF) plus a map table, assigns a new physical register to each destination at dispatch. The map table maps architectural registers to physical registers, so reads go directly to the PRF without searching the ROB. The old physical register is freed only at commit. A concrete implication: PRF designs scale to large numbers of in-flight results and faster read paths, but they need careful allocation and free list management and require map-table snapshots for recovery. A misconception is that PRF eliminates the ROB entirely; it does not. The ROB still sequences commits and records exceptions and speculation bits. The PRF simply speeds value access and removes the need to search the ROB on each register read.

keyIdea.title: ROB vs PRF
keyIdea.text: PRF with a map table accelerates reads by pointing directly to physical registers; ROB-only designs require searching the ROB for pending values.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › ROB vs PRF
ROB-only approach
  • ROB holds results until commit; register file contains only committed data.
  • Reading a register requires checking the ROB for the most recent pending write.
  • Simpler bookkeeping but slower reads and more ROB searches when many in-flight instructions exist.
PRF + map table approach
  • Allocate a new physical register at dispatch and update the map table to point architectural registers to it.
  • Reads go directly to PRF; no ROB search required for operand values.
  • Faster reads and scalable in-flight capacity, but requires map-table snapshots and free-list management for recovery.
Concluding contrast
Both approaches use the ROB for commit sequencing and exception handling. The PRF speeds reads and reduces ROB search overhead, which is why modern high-performance processors favor a PRF along with a ROB for control metadata and commit ordering.

screens.title: Speculative Execution and ROB Handling of Mispredictions
screens.narratorSegment: Speculative execution fetches and executes instructions from a predicted path before the branch outcome is known. The ROB records which entries are speculative by setting a speculation bit when entries are fetched after a predicted branch. Speculative entries may execute and write results into their ROB entries, but they cannot commit until the branch resolves and indicates the correct path. If the prediction is correct, the speculative bit is cleared and the entries can later commit normally. If the prediction is wrong, the processor flushes all speculative entries after the branch: their ROB slots are discarded and their results never reach the register file or memory. This gives a safe and efficient way to explore predicted work while retaining precise exception semantics. A common misconception is that speculative writes to memory must be allowed; stores are typically buffered and made visible only on commit to avoid leaking incorrect side effects. Consider this practical point: the ROB acts as the recovery log for speculation — by holding results and marking them speculative, it makes it straightforward to discard incorrect-path work without complex undo logic.

keyIdea.title: Speculation
keyIdea.text: Speculative entries are marked and discarded on misprediction; commit only applies correct-path results to architectural state.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Speculation & Flush

Speculative execution lifecycle

When a branch is predicted, subsequent ROB entries are marked speculative. They execute and write results to the ROB but cannot commit until the branch outcome confirms the correct path.

Prediction correct
Clear speculation bits and let entries commit in order.
Prediction wrong
Flush all speculative entries after the branch and restore the last committed state. Speculative results never reach the register file.
Pro tip
Buffer store operations so they are only applied at commit. This prevents speculative stores from changing memory visible to other agents before validation.
Example
A branch predicted taken creates speculative I3 and I4. If the prediction fails at I2's resolution, I3 and I4 are flushed from the ROB and never commit.
Check
How does the ROB let you undo speculative work without complex rollback mechanisms? Because results were never made architectural.

screens.title: ROB Interaction with Reservation Stations and Register File
screens.narratorSegment: The ROB, reservation stations, and register file form a small ecosystem for in-flight values. At dispatch an instruction is placed in a reservation station and allocated a ROB slot. The reservation station holds operand tags that refer to either ROB entries or committed registers. When operands are ready, the instruction executes in the reservation station and writes its result into the ROB entry and sets the ready bit. Meanwhile, the architectural register file remains unchanged. At commit, the ROB writes the ready value into the register file or commits a store to memory. In PRF designs, the register map table points architectural registers to physical registers allocated at dispatch; execution writes directly into the physical register, and the ROB still coordinates commit and records exceptions and speculation bits. A misconception is to think the reservation station holds the only copy of the result; in fact it is transient — the ROB or PRF is the canonical uncommitted storage. Understanding these interactions clarifies why reading the latest value requires consulting the mapping or the ROB and why commit is the single place that makes changes permanent.

keyIdea.text: Reservation stations execute, ROB (or PRF) stores uncommitted results, and commit moves values to the architectural register file.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › ROB ↔ RS ↔ RF
Reservation Station
Holds instructions and operand tags. Fires when operands are ready and issues execution out of order.
Reorder Buffer
Stores results, ready bits, exceptions, and speculation markers until commit ensures architectural updates in order.
Register File / PRF
Holds committed state; with a PRF and map table, uncommitted values can be stored in a physical register allocated at dispatch.
Flow: dispatch → RS (tags) → execute → write ROB or PRF → commit → update RF / memory. The mapping between architecture and physical registers or ROB entries is what lets reads find the latest value without corrupting committed state.

screens.title: ROB Size, ILP, and the Cost of Misprediction
screens.narratorSegment: The size of the ROB determines how many instructions can be in flight between dispatch and commit. A larger ROB lets the processor keep more speculative and out-of-order work in progress, increasing the opportunity to extract instruction-level parallelism. However, a larger ROB also increases area and power and — importantly — the potential cost when a branch misprediction or exception requires flushing entries. For example, if a processor has a 128-entry ROB and a branch in the middle is mispredicted, on average roughly half the ROB might contain speculative instructions that must be discarded, costing many cycles to refill the pipeline. Designers must balance these trade-offs: larger ROBs can improve throughput on long dependency chains, but they make recovery more expensive and increase commit complexity. A common misconception is that simply increasing ROB size always improves performance; diminishing returns, longer allocation/search paths, and higher misprediction penalties often limit the benefit. Reflect on how commit bandwidth, issue width, and branch accuracy interact with ROB size to determine the real performance impact. ROB Size, ILP, and the Cost of Misprediction means larger robs increase in-flight parallelism but also raise area, power, and potential misprediction recovery costs.. In practical terms, why rob capacity matters and how it affects recovery costs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › ROB Size & ILP

Capacity and consequences

ROB size defines how many uncommitted instructions can be tracked. More entries allow deeper speculation and higher ILP extraction, especially across long dependency chains.

Benefit
Larger instruction windows can hide latencies and expose parallelism.
Cost
More area, power, complex commit logic, and larger potential flush penalties on mispredicts.
Rule of thumb
Designers weigh ILP gains against power/area and the typical cost of mispredictions for their target workloads.
Practical example
If a 128-entry ROB has a branch in the middle, on average 64 speculative instructions may be flushed, representing many wasted cycles and lost issue bandwidth.
Check your understanding

screens.title: Cycle-by-Cycle ROB Simulation: Branch Misprediction Example
screens.narratorSegment: In the hands-on activity you extend a Tomasulo simulation with an 8-entry ROB and run a trace with a predicted-taken branch that is actually not taken. The sequence is: I1 ADD R1,R2,R3; I2 BEQ R1,R2,target predicted taken but actually not; I3 ADD R4,R5,R6 speculative; I4 SUB R7,R8,R9 speculative; I5 MUL at target on the correct path. The simulator should allocate ROB entries at dispatch, execute I3 and I4 speculatively writing results into ROB slots, and then when the branch outcome is known at I2 the processor discovers the misprediction. At that point the ROB flushes I3 and I4, discarding their values, and the fetch resumes at the correct target so I5 is placed into the ROB and later committed. The penalty equals the number of cycles spent issuing, executing, or otherwise processing I3 and I4 that do not contribute to committed work. In the example above, those two speculative instructions represent wasted work and may amount to several cycles of issue and execution latency. When you run your simulator, show the ROB entries per cycle, the speculative bits, the flush moment, and the cycle count of wasted work so you can explain the misprediction cost.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Cycle Simulation
Trace
I1: ADD  R1, R2, R3
I2: BEQ  R1, R2, target    ; predicted taken, actually not taken
I3: ADD  R4, R5, R6        ; speculative on predicted path
I4: SUB  R7, R8, R9        ; speculative on predicted path
target:
I5: MUL  R10, R11, R12     ; correct-path instruction
Below is an illustrative cycle-by-cycle ROB snapshot you should produce in your simulator. Each row is a cycle; entries show index:state(spec). 'R' means ready, 'S' speculative, 'F' flushed.
Cycle 1: Tail alloc I1 -> ROB[0]: I1(R)
Cycle 1: Tail alloc I2 -> ROB[1]: I2(S?)
Cycle 2: Issue I1 executes -> ROB[0]=I1(R)
Cycle 2: Issue I2 decodes, predicted taken -> fetch predicted path
Cycle 3: Tail alloc I3 -> ROB[2]: I3(S)
Cycle 3: I3 executes out-of-order -> ROB[2]=I3(R,S)
Cycle 4: Tail alloc I4 -> ROB[3]: I4(S)
Cycle 4: I4 executes -> ROB[3]=I4(R,S)
Cycle 5: Branch I2 resolves: predicted taken was wrong -> flush ROB entries after I2
After flush: ROB[2]=F, ROB[3]=F (I3 and I4 discarded)
Cycle 6: Fetch target, Tail alloc I5 -> ROB[2]: I5
Cycle 7+: I5 executes and commits in-order when head reaches it
Penalty calculation
I3 and I4 represent wasted work. The total penalty equals the cycles spent issuing and executing them plus cycles to refill the pipeline; measure these directly in your simulator.
Simulation checklist
  • Allocate ROB entries at dispatch in program order
  • Write execution results to ROB and set ready
  • Commit only at head and flush on mispredict
Expected outcome
Your trace should show I3 and I4 marked speculative then flushed, and the register file should never receive their results.

screens.title: Assessment: Why PRF + Map Table Outperforms ROB-Only Reads
screens.narratorSegment: A typical assessment asks why a physical register file with a register map table provides better performance than a design where the ROB stores all uncommitted values. The key reason is access speed and complexity: in a ROB-only design, a register read must search the ROB to find the latest pending write for that architectural register. Searching a large ROB every read is slow and energy intensive. In contrast, a PRF with a map table points directly to the physical register holding the most recent value, so reads are a single register-file access. The PRF also supports many more in-flight registers, which helps wide superscalar designs. However, the PRF imposes additional complexity: allocation and free-list management, and maintaining map-table state or checkpoints for recovery. When answering the assessment, include a concrete comparison: reading register R requires either an ROB scan or a map-table lookup plus one PRF access. Also discuss the recovery cost: a ROB-only design relies on ROB contents for recovery, while a PRF design must restore the map table on flush. A thoughtful answer weighs both read latency and recovery complexity and notes why modern high-performance processors favor PRF despite the bookkeeping overhead.

Assessment: PRF vs ROB-only

Explain why PRF designs typically yield better read performance than ROB-only approaches, and discuss costs.

Make the argument
Highlight that a PRF read is a single register-file access after a map-table lookup, while a ROB-only read may require searching the ROB for the newest pending write.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential ideas you should remember. First, imprecise exceptions occur when out-of-order completion makes it impossible to present the OS with a program-order-consistent state. Second, the Reorder Buffer (ROB) holds results and control metadata and enforces in-order commit, enabling precise exceptions and simple recovery. Third, each ROB entry contains instruction type, destination, value, ready, exception status, and a speculation bit; this metadata is what makes correct commits and flushes possible. Fourth, there are two main register interaction models: ROB-only designs that require searching the ROB for pending values, and PRF plus map-table designs that point reads directly to physical registers. Finally, ROB size trades off ILP extraction against area, power, and misprediction recovery cost. Keep these ideas in mind when you design or extend a simulator or when you reason about a processor's microarchitecture.

Imprecise exceptions
Out-of-order writes can hide the faulting instruction; precise handling requires in-order visibility.
Reorder Buffer
Circular buffer storing results, ready bits, exception and speculation flags until commit.

fullNarratorScript:
Out-of-order execution improves performance by letting independent instructions run ahead, but it complicates how we handle exceptions and branch mispredictions. In this lesson you will learn why imprecise exceptions happen when instructions complete out of program order, and how a Reorder Buffer, or ROB, holds results until they may be safely committed in program order. We will study the fields inside a ROB entry — type, destination, value, ready and speculation bits — and follow the three main phases: dispatch, execute, and commit. You will also see why modern designs use a physical register file with a map table instead of relying only on the ROB for recent values. Finally, we will work through a hands-on simulation of a mispredicted branch so you can see how speculative entries are flushed and how a recovery penalty accumulates. By the end you should be able to explain the ROB's role in precise exceptions and how it supports speculative execution while keeping the architectural state consistent. Consider how ROB size impacts both parallelism and the cost of a misprediction — that trade-off motivates many design choices in real processors.

In this lesson set you will gain four concrete skills. First, you will explain why out-of-order execution complicates exception handling: specifically, how later instructions can alter the architectural state before an earlier fault is detected, producing imprecise exceptions. Second, you will implement a reorder buffer that preserves program order for commits while letting instructions execute out of order; this includes allocating ROB entries at dispatch and writing results into the ROB rather than the register file. Third, you will understand the interaction between the ROB, reservation stations, and the register file or a physical register file with a map table; you'll see how the ROB can be the only place holding a result until commit or how a PRF lets reads bypass the ROB. Fourth, you will describe speculative execution behavior and how the ROB handles mispredictions by marking speculative entries and flushing them on branch resolution. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify your understanding by tracing a misprediction and explaining the recovery steps.

This second objectives slide focuses on what you will demonstrate when you extend a Tomasulo simulator to include a ROB. You should be able to allocate and free ROB entries correctly, store execution results in ROB entries instead of the register file, and implement a commit loop that advances the head pointer only when the head entry is ready. You will also implement a flush operation that discards all entries after a mispredicted branch or an exception at the head, restoring the map table or register file to the last committed state. Finally, you will run a cycle-by-cycle simulation with a predicted-taken branch that is mispredicted and measure the penalty by counting cycles lost while speculative instructions are flushed and state is restored. These abilities show you understand both the microarchitectural motivation and the practical code paths needed to make a precise, recoverable pipeline.

An imprecise exception occurs when the processor can no longer guarantee which instruction caused a fault because later instructions have already modified the architectural state. In a sequential design, an exception arises when the offending instruction completes and the processor stops in program order. In contrast, an out-of-order engine may execute and even write results for younger instructions before an older instruction raises an exception. A concrete example: imagine instruction five causes a divide-by-zero, but instruction eight has already written its result to a register. If the processor cannot undo instruction eight's write, the register file no longer reflects the state at the point of instruction five, and the operating system cannot reconstruct a correct program state. That is why imprecise exceptions are unacceptable for general-purpose systems. A common misconception is that simply stopping execution later will be sufficient; it is not, because writes already made by younger instructions persist unless the architecture prevents or delays them. The ROB solves this by buffering writes until commit. Think about this question: if you could snapshot every register at every instruction, would you still need a ROB? The practical cost of full snapshots explains why the ROB is the preferred lightweight solution.

A Reorder Buffer is a circular, program-ordered buffer that holds instructions from dispatch until commit. Each entry records the instruction type, destination architectural register, computed value, a ready bit indicating execution completion, an exception flag, and a speculation bit. The ROB's central role is to allow instruction execution to proceed out of order while deferring writes to the architectural state until it is safe to apply them in program order. This guarantees precise exceptions and enables simple recovery: if an exception or a misprediction is detected at the head, the processor can flush all later entries without having to undo committed state. A common misconception is that the ROB stores only values; in practice it stores control status too, like exception flags and speculation markers, which are essential for deciding whether to commit an entry. The ROB is a circular structure with head and tail pointers; the tail allocates new entries at dispatch and the head advances on commit. Consider a high-level analogy: the ROB is like a waiting room that records results out of order but only lets people through the exit in order.

Dispatch and execution are the first two stages of ROB operation. At dispatch, the processor allocates a ROB entry in program order and places the instruction in a reservation station. The destination register is marked as being produced by that ROB entry, so reads of that architectural register will either read a committed value or the pending ROB result. Execution can proceed out of order inside reservation stations; when an instruction completes there, it writes the computed value into its ROB entry and sets the ready bit. Importantly, the result is not written into the architectural register file at this moment. A concrete example: an ADD dispatched as entry 5 executes earlier than entry 3 in the reservation station and writes its sum into ROB[5]. Later, commit logic will allow ROB[3] and then ROB[5] to write to registers. A common misconception is that reserving the destination in the register file makes writes atomic; instead the ROB keeps the architectural file unchanged until commit. The dispatch/execute split enables high instruction-level parallelism while preserving an ordered commit path for correctness. ROB Operation: Dispatch and Execute means dispatch allocates an ordered rob slot; execute writes results to the rob and sets ready bits without touching architectural state.. In practical terms, how instructions enter the rob and write results back. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Commit is the stage where the ROB enforces program order on architectural updates. The commit logic repeatedly checks the head entry: if the head's ready bit is set and no exception is recorded, the ROB writes the entry's value into the register file or commits a store to memory, then advances the head pointer to the next entry. If the head entry has an exception, the processor handles the exception using the precise state at the previous commit point and flushes all subsequent ROB entries. For branch mispredictions, when the branch resolves at or before commit and is found incorrect, all speculative entries after that branch are discarded. A flush discards results stored only in the ROB and restores the register map or register file to match the last committed state. A common error in implementations is to forget to free resources or update the map table only after commit; doing those steps incorrectly breaks recoverability. Think of commit as a gatekeeper: only when the gate opens does the ROB's data become part of the architectural state. What decision does commit make if the head is not ready? It stalls and preserves precise ordering until the instruction completes.

There are two common approaches to holding in-flight results: keeping the ROB as the only source of pending results, or using a physical register file with a register map table. In the ROB-with-register-file approach, the ROB stores results until commit, and the register file always reflects only committed values. Reading a register requires checking the ROB to find the most recent uncommitted write. This searching can be slow and power hungry. The alternative, a Physical Register File (PRF) plus a map table, assigns a new physical register to each destination at dispatch. The map table maps architectural registers to physical registers, so reads go directly to the PRF without searching the ROB. The old physical register is freed only at commit. A concrete implication: PRF designs scale to large numbers of in-flight results and faster read paths, but they need careful allocation and free list management and require map-table snapshots for recovery. A misconception is that PRF eliminates the ROB entirely; it does not. The ROB still sequences commits and records exceptions and speculation bits. The PRF simply speeds value access and removes the need to search the ROB on each register read.

Speculative execution fetches and executes instructions from a predicted path before the branch outcome is known. The ROB records which entries are speculative by setting a speculation bit when entries are fetched after a predicted branch. Speculative entries may execute and write results into their ROB entries, but they cannot commit until the branch resolves and indicates the correct path. If the prediction is correct, the speculative bit is cleared and the entries can later commit normally. If the prediction is wrong, the processor flushes all speculative entries after the branch: their ROB slots are discarded and their results never reach the register file or memory. This gives a safe and efficient way to explore predicted work while retaining precise exception semantics. A common misconception is that speculative writes to memory must be allowed; stores are typically buffered and made visible only on commit to avoid leaking incorrect side effects. Consider this practical point: the ROB acts as the recovery log for speculation — by holding results and marking them speculative, it makes it straightforward to discard incorrect-path work without complex undo logic.

The ROB, reservation stations, and register file form a small ecosystem for in-flight values. At dispatch an instruction is placed in a reservation station and allocated a ROB slot. The reservation station holds operand tags that refer to either ROB entries or committed registers. When operands are ready, the instruction executes in the reservation station and writes its result into the ROB entry and sets the ready bit. Meanwhile, the architectural register file remains unchanged. At commit, the ROB writes the ready value into the register file or commits a store to memory. In PRF designs, the register map table points architectural registers to physical registers allocated at dispatch; execution writes directly into the physical register, and the ROB still coordinates commit and records exceptions and speculation bits. A misconception is to think the reservation station holds the only copy of the result; in fact it is transient — the ROB or PRF is the canonical uncommitted storage. Understanding these interactions clarifies why reading the latest value requires consulting the mapping or the ROB and why commit is the single place that makes changes permanent.

The size of the ROB determines how many instructions can be in flight between dispatch and commit. A larger ROB lets the processor keep more speculative and out-of-order work in progress, increasing the opportunity to extract instruction-level parallelism. However, a larger ROB also increases area and power and — importantly — the potential cost when a branch misprediction or exception requires flushing entries. For example, if a processor has a 128-entry ROB and a branch in the middle is mispredicted, on average roughly half the ROB might contain speculative instructions that must be discarded, costing many cycles to refill the pipeline. Designers must balance these trade-offs: larger ROBs can improve throughput on long dependency chains, but they make recovery more expensive and increase commit complexity. A common misconception is that simply increasing ROB size always improves performance; diminishing returns, longer allocation/search paths, and higher misprediction penalties often limit the benefit. Reflect on how commit bandwidth, issue width, and branch accuracy interact with ROB size to determine the real performance impact. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Third, 'PRF speeds reads' — a physical register file plus a map table provides direct reads to the latest value and avoids searching the ROB. These short mnemonics help you recall why the ROB exists, how it supports recovery, and why modern CPUs pair it with a PRF for performance.
